title: Your breaking rule
hookLine: write what you'll do when it breaks: the broken tablets were kept in the ark beside the whole ones
tomorrow: what did Hindu tradition call the years when you're a student?

lines: A CRACKED BOWL ON THE SHELF.
WRITTEN WITH THE FINGER OF GOD.
BROKEN AT THE FOOT OF THE MOUNTAIN.
TWO TABLES LIKE UNTO THE FIRST.
cards: Some families keep a cracked bowl on the shelf long after it stops holding soup. Moses came down the mountain with two tablets of stone, "written with the finger of God."
He saw the people dancing around a golden calf, and he threw the tablets down and broke them at the foot of the mountain. Later God told him: "Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first."
New tablets, the same words. So what happened to the broken ones?

teach.h: WHICH THOU BRAKEST, PUT THEM IN THE ARK.
teach.b: The Torah's plain words don't settle it. The rabbis read one verse closely: "which thou brakest, and thou shalt put them in the ark."
Them, they taught, means both: the whole tablets, and the broken pieces of the first, side by side.
And they drew a teaching from it: honor an old scholar who has forgotten his learning through no fault of his own, because the broken tablets were kept in the ark too.
That's the Jewish teaching of the broken tablets: what breaks isn't thrown out. It's carried with the whole.
This whole stretch has been about breaking: dry seasons, busy ones, illness, grief, doubt, boredom, missed days, a raft outgrown, a life that changes, a practice wound too tight.

teach.h: ONE PAGE FOR EACH KIND OF BREAK.
teach.b: A breaking rule is one page that says what you'll do when each comes. Keep one thing. Shrink it.
Just breathe. Start again at one, without a speech. And keep the broken pieces with the new.

how: Jewish tradition, from the Talmud, holds that the broken first tablets were kept in the ark beside the second, and draws from it honor for elders who have forgotten their learning. On a personal rule, a breaking rule is a short page saying what to keep and how to restart when practice breaks.

games.q: your grandmother, once a great cook, can't remember her recipes anymore and says she's no use in the kitchen now. what fits the teaching of the broken tablets?
o: she still belongs at the center, like the broken tablets kept in the ark.
let her rest somewhere else; the kitchen is for those who remember.
write the recipes down so no one needs her anymore.
games.why: the rabbis taught honor for the scholar who forgot through no fault of his own, because the broken tablets lay in the ark beside the whole.

practice: Write your breaking rule in a few short lines: what you'll keep in a dry season, a busy one, a sick one, a grieving one, and how you'll start again.
Then fold it and set it with your other pages, broken weeks included, until the bell.
